newsitem.title: UK: BA denies slot sacrifice report for AA deal.
newsitem.headline: BA denies slot sacrifice report for AA deal.

text.p: British Airways on Sunday denied a newspaper report that it may offer to surrender some prime take-off and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport in order to secure a global alliance with American Airlines.

The Sunday Times newspaper reported that the airline companies had accepted that slot concessions would be needed to clinch the deal in a move that coincided with growing forecasts that the UK and American governments would reach an open-skies agreement to liberalise air travel between the two countries.
But a British Airways (BA) spokesman dismissed the article.

"We see no reason for undertakings of any kind," he told Reuters. "Our European rivals have not had to make them so why should we? The proposed alliance is good for competition and it's good for customers."

The Sunday Times, which noted that officially the two carriers had a "no surrender" position on slots, said that sacrificing landing slots would defuse opposition from other airlines and authorities on both sides of the Atlantic.

British Airways and American Airlines (AA) announced in June that they were forging the world's largest airline alliance in the biggest of the current wave of link-ups in the airline industry that sparked furious opposition from other airlines.

U.S. officials have said that they would not approve the alliance, that would give BA and AA about 60 percent of traffic between the UK and U.S., until there is a "meaningful" open-skies agreement across the Atlantic.
But the U.S. called off the latest round of talks with Britain about two weeks ago, with the prized issue of Heathrow landing slots cited as one of the major sticking points.

The U.S. wants access for all U.S. carriers to Heathrow, Europe's most popular airport. Another major hurdle in the talks is the U.S. demands for rights for its carriers to fly from Britain to other European countries.

In return for opening up Heathrow, British carriers, including BA, want the U.S. to raise its 25 percent ceiling on foreign ownership of airlines -- thereby allowing British airlines access to the giant U.S. domestic air passenger market.
